A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SeRL research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaMA and Qwen experiments on mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro, together with reward-hacking, reward-alignment, and generated-data analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds filtering ablations, SFT comparisons, longer training experiments, medical-domain evaluations, and additional reward comparisons.

M1.justification: SeRL retains online instruction generation, the same four filtering components, majority-voting rewards, shortest-response tie-breaking, and iterative RL updates. The expanded implementation description and revised Reinforce++ equations do not establish a change to the implemented SeRL procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds an actual medical-domain training and evaluation setting: MedQA supplies seed instructions, and evaluation covers MedQA, PubMedQA, and NephSAP (Appendix D.3). This substantially extends the mathematical training and math/general-reasoning evaluations retained from v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds SFT baselines using majority responses, correct responses, and responses distilled from Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct (Table 8). Its reward-alignment comparison additionally evaluates entropy-based and CAI rewards (Table 11). These extend the actual comparator sets; the original I-RPO, SR-DPO, and RL-GT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include equal-step filtering ablations, training through six iterations, and medical training with 500 seed instructions against a full-10.2k-data baseline. Reward alignment gains MAE and MSE metrics. Section 4.1 also replaces the approximate 100-steps-per-7,500-instructions budget description with matched gradient steps; this reported revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds individual filtering-component ablations (Table 3), filtered training curves alongside the existing unfiltered curves (Figure 2), analysis of convergence through iterations 4-6 (Table 9), and broader reward-reliability comparisons (Table 11). The original reward-hacking case study, RL-MV ablation, RL-algorithm comparison, and generated-data analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark performance. The instruction-length and quality summaries with plus/minus values are unchanged between v1 Table 7 and v2 Table 12. The new reward-error metrics do not constitute uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces v1's duplicated Qwen MMLU-Pro values: its initial average changes from 34.0 to 57.3, and iteration-3 average from 35.1 to 57.4. New Tables 3 and 8-11 add filtering, SFT, extended-iteration, medical, and reward-alignment results. Original Table 1 math scores remain unchanged; the revised Qwen entries should not be interpreted as a cross-version training gain.

T1.justification: Equation 1 changes the sampling distribution in the objective from the current policy to the old policy. Appendix C.1 replaces v1's return expression with accumulated reward/KL expressions and a terminal-reward derivation, alongside explicit advantage-normalization formulas. These are limited mathematical revisions to the existing RL exposition, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstracts, contribution lists, and conclusions retain the same central claims: combining self-instruction and majority-voting rewards enables RL from limited data, outperforms iterative counterparts, and approaches training with extensive labeled data. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses limitations for open-ended writing and process-sensitive tasks such as proofs, and interprets difficulty filtering as curriculum learning that reduces reward-estimation bias. It revises explanations of Reinforce++ robustness toward batch normalization and RLOO's amplification of reward errors, and further qualifies iterative improvement as capacity-limited. The main interpretation of SeRL's benefits remains intact.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents the ROUGE-L threshold of 0.7, 3-150-word limits, fuller keyword and initial-character exclusion rules, the one-quarter seed/three-quarter generated few-shot mixture, and the CoT sampling prompt. It also clarifies SR-DPO's reward-model identity, while Section 4.1 specifies the evaluation token limit. These address substantial implementation gaps. The abstract's public code link remains, while the additional anonymous link is removed.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds substantive positioning against WizardLM, TeaMs-RL, and RLSC, and the bibliography gains supporting RL and medical references. The central positioning relative to self-instruction, self-rewarding, and TTRL remains. Citation renumbering and publication-metadata updates are not substantive research-positioning changes.

P1.justification: Most of the introduction, method narrative, and conclusion remain closely matched. v2 standardizes terminology, edits selected explanations, labels the ablation subsections, moves Reinforce++ exposition into Appendix C.1, and adds an appendix contents page and expanded subsection structure. Affiliations and acknowledgements also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular displays for filtering components, SFT strategies, extended iterations, medical benchmarks, and reward alignment (Tables 3 and 8-11). Figure 2 becomes a direct filtered/unfiltered training comparison. Existing benchmark highlighting is simplified, prompt displays are relabeled as boxes, and appendix figures are redistributed while retaining their underlying analyses.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the paper's central design and applicability: controlled filter ablations test previously unisolated components, and medical experiments extend validation beyond mathematical training. It also repairs the duplicated Qwen results, supplies important reproduction details, and better states applicability and iteration limits. Run-level uncertainty remains absent, and Table 11 does not explain how its majority-reward MAE/MSE values relate to the stated binary rewards. These reporting weaknesses temper individual findings but do not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.
